periods.activity_title: Defining Work from Lifting Wheat Bags to the Formula
periods.section_anchor: 7.1 Work Done by a Constant Force

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: two workers carry wheat bags — one lifts twice as many bags to the same height, another lifts the same number to twice the height. Which worker does more work, and why? Students write a one-sentence prediction individually before any discussion.

Introduce the formal definition W = F × s. Students work in pairs on two quick calculations: (a) a 50 N force moves an object 3 m — find work done; (b) a 100 N force acts but the object does not move — find work done. Pairs share answers and reconcile any differences.

Project or draw the force-displacement graph. Students shade the area under the graph for a constant-force scenario and state what the area represents. Then pose: what would the graph look like if force varied? Students sketch a rough variable-force graph and argue why area-under-graph still gives work.

Class discussion: students articulate in their own words why both the magnitude of force AND displacement in the direction of force must be non-zero for work to be done. Teacher consolidates by writing W = F × s and the unit joule (J) on the board with a clear derivation of the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's entry point; start by surfacing the gap between the everyday word 'work' and its scientific meaning before writing any formula. A common error is treating any force as doing work — watch for students who claim that a larger force always means more work regardless of displacement. A useful checkpoint: ask a student to explain why holding a heavy book at arm's length for a long time is tiring but involves zero scientific work.
homework: A 30 N force pulls a trolley 4 m along a flat surface, and separately, a 15 N force pushes the same trolley 8 m. Calculate work done in each case and explain which force was more effective at doing work per newton applied.

periods.activity_title: Three Conditions for Zero Work and the Effort Paradox
periods.section_anchor: 7.1.1 When is work done equal to zero?
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing force and displacement vectors for three zero-work scenarios

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks through three conditions for zero work: (i) force is zero, (ii) displacement is zero (pushing a rigid wall), (iii) force is perpendicular to displacement (carrying a box horizontally while applying an upward supporting force). For each, teacher draws the force and displacement vectors on the board.

Students individually analyse the Pause and Ponder scenarios: (a) a weightlifter holding a barbell steady overhead — which work conditions apply? (b) friction acting on a sliding stack of coins — is the work positive, negative, or zero? Students write a justification for each before a whole-class share.

Teacher introduces the distinction between physiological effort and scientific work: muscles deplete internal chemical energy even when zero work is done on the held object. Students discuss in pairs: where does the energy go if not into the barbell? (heat, muscle micro-contraction). Teacher draws out the key idea that internal energy expenditure is real but is not scientific work done on the external object.

Quick consolidation: teacher poses three rapid scenarios on the board and students vote (thumbs up/down/sideways) on whether each is zero-work and which condition applies. Teacher corrects misconceptions on the spot.

periods.teacher_notes: The perpendicular-force condition is the hardest of the three for students — they intuitively feel that supporting a load while walking must involve work on the load. Having established that work requires force in the direction of displacement, connect this to the box-carrying scenario explicitly and ask students which direction the supporting force points versus which way the box moves. Watch for the misconception that 'if I feel tired, I must be doing work on the object'; the physiological-effort discussion directly addresses this. A probing question: ask students whether a planet orbiting the Sun does work against gravity.

periods.activity_title: Positive and Negative Work — Direction Decides the Sign
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of goalkeeper scenario showing force and displacement vectors

time_bands.activity: Students read the goalkeeper example from the textbook independently. They then draw a vector diagram showing the football's displacement and the goalkeeper's force on the ball, labelling the directions. A student volunteer shares their diagram for class critique.

Students work the two textbook worked examples: (a) a girl lifts then lowers a dumbbell — calculate work done in each phase and determine the sign; (b) goalkeeper exerts 200 N over 15 cm — compute work done. Students must write the sign convention rule in their own words after completing the calculations.

Teacher introduces Newton's third law implication: both the ball and the goalkeeper do work on each other simultaneously, with opposite signs. Students draw both action-reaction force pairs and explain in one sentence why the signs differ. Whole-class discussion reconciles any confusion about whose work is being measured.
Exit exercise: students write one original real-life example of negative work (not from the textbook) and justify the sign using direction of force relative to displacement.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that work depends on force in the direction of displacement, the sign of work is a natural extension — force and displacement in opposite directions give a negative product. A frequent error is treating negative work as 'no work done'; stress that negative work is real work that removes energy from the object. The Newton's third law extension is genuinely surprising: ask students to identify who is doing positive and negative work in the goalkeeper scenario from each object's perspective before revealing the answer.

periods.activity_title: The Work-Energy Theorem — Tracing Energy Transfers Through Collisions
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of carrom shot energy-transfer sequence

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the cricket-ball-and-wicket scenario: a thrown ball demolishes the stumps. Where did the ability to do that come from? Students brainstorm in pairs, then the class converges on the idea that the work done on the ball gave it the capacity to do work on the stumps. Teacher formalises: energy is the capacity to do work.

Teacher presents the work-energy theorem W = ΔE on the board, explaining that positive work increases an object's energy and negative work decreases it. Students apply the theorem to the flowerpot falling from a height: identify the force doing work, determine the sign, and state what happens to the pot's energy.

Students trace the carrom-shot energy transfer chain from textbook — striker hits white coin, white coin hits black coin — identifying at each collision which object does positive work and which receives negative work, and applying Newton's third law to justify the signs.

Pause and Ponder: students map the energy forms when pedalling a bicycle on a flat road (chemical → mechanical → kinetic, with some thermal via friction). Students share and the class agrees on the complete chain.

periods.teacher_notes: The work-energy theorem links the two halves of the chapter: work (just defined) gives rise to energy change. Watch for students who think energy is a substance transferred rather than a capacity — the carrom example is effective because no substance moves from coin to coin, only the capacity to do work. Ask students to state W = ΔE in plain language before accepting the symbolic form as understood.
homework: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is thrown upward, slowing down as it rises. Using the work-energy theorem, explain whether the work done by gravity on the ball is positive or negative during the upward journey, and what happens to the ball's energy.

periods.activity_title: Forms of Energy — Conversions Across Mechanical and Other Types

time_bands.activity: Students individually list as many forms of energy as they can from memory in two minutes. Class pool is collected on the board. Teacher guides students to match each form to a concrete object or process, checking against the chapter's list: mechanical, thermal, light, sound, electrical, nuclear, chemical.

Students work in small groups to construct an energy-conversion chain for three everyday examples: (a) a ringing electric bell, (b) eating food and riding a bicycle, (c) a burning candle. Each group draws a flow diagram showing the form at each step and the conversion happening between steps.

Groups share diagrams. Teacher draws a composite flowchart on the board, highlighting that the chapter focuses on mechanical energy specifically because it links directly to the forces and motions already studied.

Students answer: why does mechanical energy deserve its own detailed study in this chapter rather than being listed alongside the others? They connect the answer to the work-energy theorem established earlier.

periods.teacher_notes: The work-energy theorem (W = ΔE) is the bridge from this section to mechanical energy — every form of energy in this section is converted from or to mechanical energy in everyday life. Watch for students who treat light and heat as the 'end' of any energy chain and cannot identify further conversions; this is a common stopping point. Encourage groups to ask: what could this form of energy do if it acted on an object, to reinforce the definition of energy as capacity to do work.

periods.activity_title: Deriving Kinetic Energy from Newton's Laws and Kinematics
periods.visual_aids: Board derivation layout showing each algebraic step

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads the derivation of K = ½mv² on the board, explicitly showing each step: start from W = F × s, substitute F = ma (Newton's second law), substitute s from v² = u² + 2as, simplify to get W = ½mv² − ½mu². Students copy the derivation and annotate each step with the law or formula used.

Students work the textbook worked examples individually: (a) compare kinetic energy when velocity doubles (find the ratio K₂/K₁); (b) calculate kinetic energy of a cricket ball bowled at 154.8 km h⁻¹ (convert to m s⁻¹ first, then apply K = ½mv²).

Teacher presents the jet-aircraft stopping problem (367,500 N over 100 m). Students first use the work-energy theorem to find kinetic energy, then solve for landing speed. Teacher checks that students apply the sign convention correctly (negative work removes energy).

Pause and Ponder: two objects with the same kinetic energy but masses m and 4m — which has greater speed, and by what factor? Students derive the ratio from K = ½mv² algebraically before answering. Also: does kinetic energy change if an object moves at constant velocity? Students reason from the work-energy theorem.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivation depends on the kinematics equation v² = u² + 2as — if students are uncertain about this, write it on the board and confirm its origin before substituting. A common algebraic error is forgetting the factor of ½; step through the cancellation of the factor 2 from 2as explicitly. The 'same KE, different mass' Pause and Ponder is a good check — students who cannot rearrange K = ½mv² for v need individual support before the next section.

periods.activity_title: Potential Energy — Stored Energy in Deformed and Elevated Objects
materials: Heavy ball (e.g. large steel ball or cricket ball)

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates (or students observe) a stretched rubber band being released — it shoots a paper pellet. Class identifies that the stored energy before release becomes kinetic energy after. Students brainstorm three more examples of deformation storing energy (spring, bent ruler, compressed ball).

Activity 7.1: Students drop the heavy ball into the sand tray from 1 m height, mark and measure the depression depth. Then drop from 2 m and compare. Students record results in a table and write one sentence explaining what the depression depth indicates about stored energy before release.

Teacher derives U = mgh on the board using the work-energy theorem: force needed to raise mass m at constant speed = mg; work done over height h = mgh = energy stored. Students work the textbook example (200 g cricket ball thrown 10 m high → 20 J) independently.

Teacher broadens the concept: any system where gravitational, electric, or magnetic forces act between objects stores potential energy due to relative positions. Students write one sentence each for gravitational, elastic, and magnetic potential energy giving the source of storage in each case.

periods.teacher_notes: The sand-drop activity provides direct evidence that greater height means greater stored energy before students see the formula — run Activity 7.1 before the derivation so the algebra explains what they observed, not the other way round. A typical error is writing U = mgh and treating m in grams rather than kilograms; insist on SI units at every step. Watch for students who think potential energy 'disappears' when the object is released — the conversion to kinetic energy should be made explicit at the close.

periods.activity_title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy — Algebraic Proof and Pendulum Evidence
materials: Small heavy bob (metal nut or small metal ball)
Tape or hook to fix to ceiling/wall
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram tracking KE and PE at five positions of a freely falling object

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the algebraic proof on the board: freely falling object at height h has E = mgh; at intermediate time t, PE = mgh − ½mg²t², KE = ½mg²t², total = mgh at every point. Students copy the proof, filling in the step that uses v = gt (velocity under free fall) and substituting into K = ½mv².

Activity 7.2: Students set up a simple pendulum, mark the release height on both sides, and release the bob. They observe whether it rises to the same height on the other side. Students record the actual heights and note any discrepancy, then explain the shortfall using the concept of friction at the support and air resistance.

Students work the two textbook worked examples: (a) an object slides down a frictionless ramp of height h — derive its speed at the bottom using conservation (v = √(2gh), independent of mass and path); (b) find the minimum ramp length to stop the 10,000 kg truck (72 km h⁻¹, 50,000 N friction, 30° incline).

Pause and Ponder: students calculate total mechanical energy of a falling ball just before impact and verify it equals mgh. Then they trace KE and PE at several points on a roller-coaster and explain why successive peaks must be lower when friction is present.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived both KE = ½mv² and U = mgh separately, the conservation proof brings them together — highlight that the sum mgh remains constant at every position. The pendulum activity rarely gives perfect height equality; rather than treating this as experimental error to apologise for, use it as evidence that real machines always lose some mechanical energy to friction and air resistance, connecting to simple machines later. A probing question: ask students whether conservation of mechanical energy holds on the Moon — the formula changes but the principle does not.
homework: A ball is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved ramp of height 5 m. Using conservation of mechanical energy, calculate its speed at the bottom. Then explain what would change if the ramp had friction, and in which direction the actual speed would differ from your calculated value.

periods.activity_title: Power — Rate of Doing Work and Its Practical Consequences

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses: two students carry identical loads up the same staircase — one runs, one walks. Who does more work? Students answer and justify. Teacher confirms the work is identical, then asks what is different. Class converges on: the time taken. Teacher defines power as P = W/t and gives the unit watt (W).

Students work both textbook examples independently: (a) weightlifter raises 75 kg by 2 m in 5 s — compute work done then power; (b) car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from rest to 72 km h⁻¹ in 10 s — find kinetic energy gained, then average engine power. Students compare both answers and rank the tasks by power requirement.

Students design a quick inquiry: how could they measure their own stair-climbing power using only a ruler, a stopwatch, and a bathroom scale? They write the method and the formula they would use, identifying what to measure and what to calculate.

Class discussion: why do high-power machines not necessarily do more total work? Students articulate that power is about rate — a higher-power engine does the same job faster, not more total work. Teacher links back to P = W/t and confirms the distinction.

periods.teacher_notes: The stair-climbing scenario is familiar and effective; build the definition from the contrast rather than stating it. A frequent confusion is between work and power — students sometimes write that a more powerful engine 'does more work', which is only true if time is held constant. The student-designed measurement activity is worth taking seriously: the method they describe (measuring height climbed, body weight, and time) is exactly how power is measured in a real experiment.

periods.activity_title: Simple Machines — Mechanical Advantage and Why Machines Cannot Create Energy
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing effort, load, and mechanical advantage ratio

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces simple machines as force-modifying or direction-changing devices. Key vocabulary is established: effort, load, mechanical advantage (MA = load/effort). Students write a concise definition of each term in their own words before the teacher confirms the formal version.

Teacher explains the fundamental constraint — total work is conserved, not reduced. Students compute: if MA = 4 (load four times effort), the effort must move through four times the distance the load moves. Students verify this using W = F × s for both the effort side and the load side, confirming effort × distance = load × distance.

Students generate two columns on their paper: 'What a machine CAN do' (change force magnitude, change direction) and 'What a machine CANNOT do' (reduce total work, create energy). They populate each column with examples and non-examples drawn from the textbook section, then share with a partner.

Teacher previews the three machines to be studied (pulley, inclined plane, lever) by asking students to predict for each: does it mainly change force magnitude, direction, or both? Students record predictions to revisit after studying each machine.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit establishes the conceptual framework that all three subsequent machine studies depend on — MA, effort, load, and work conservation. A persistent misconception is that machines make work easier by reducing the total work required; establish firmly that they redistribute effort over distance, not reduce energy. Ask students to articulate why a perpetual motion machine is impossible before they encounter the lever's Pause and Ponder, so they arrive at that section with the energy-conservation constraint already active.

periods.activity_title: Fixed and Movable Pulleys — Direction Change Versus Force Reduction
materials: Small weight or bag of sand
Hook or beam to suspend pulley (improvised if no pulley available — use a smooth round rod)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of fixed and movable pulley systems

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates (or draws on board) a fixed pulley: one end of a rope over a smooth rod, weight on one side, student pulls the other side down. Class observes that the force needed equals the weight (MA = 1) but the direction of pull changes from up to down. Students record the observation and state what the fixed pulley changes and what it does not change.

Teacher demonstrates or draws a movable pulley system attached to the load. Students observe that the load is supported by two rope segments, so each bears half the load, and the effort equals half the load weight. Students calculate MA for the movable pulley system using MA = load/effort and verify MA > 1.

Students apply the work-conservation principle to both systems: in the movable pulley, effort is halved but effort-rope moves twice as far as the load. Students verify numerically: if load = 100 N lifted 1 m, effort = 50 N but must pull 2 m, confirming work done is identical. They connect this to the general MA principle from Section 7.6.

Students revisit their prediction from the previous unit about whether pulleys mainly change force, direction, or both, correct their prediction if needed, and write one sentence each for fixed and movable pulleys stating what advantage each provides and at what cost.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that MA = load/effort and that work is conserved, the fixed-versus-movable contrast becomes a direct application — MA = 1 for fixed, MA > 1 for movable. A common error is thinking that movable pulleys reduce total work; return students to the calculation showing that effort × effort-distance = load × load-distance. Real-life applications (elevators, cranes) motivate why the direction change of a fixed pulley is itself useful even at MA = 1.

periods.activity_title: Inclined Plane — Measuring How Slope Angle Changes Required Force
materials: Small toy cart or block with hook
Stack of books to vary plank height
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of inclined plane with effort and height labelled

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the problem: you need to load a heavy barrel onto a truck. You could lift it vertically 1 m (very hard) or roll it up a ramp. Why is the ramp easier? Students predict whether force increases or decreases as the ramp gets steeper, and record predictions before handling apparatus.

Activity 7.3: Students set up the plank at three different heights (low, medium, steep) using book stacks. For each, they use the spring balance to measure the force needed to pull the cart up the plank at constant speed. They record length of plank (L), height raised (h), force measured (F′), and weight of cart (mg) in a table, then compute MA = mg/F′ for each slope.

Teacher derives the inclined-plane MA formula from the work-energy theorem: F′ × L = mg × h, so MA = L/h. Students compare their experimental MA values to L/h and discuss sources of discrepancy (friction between cart and plank).

Pause and Ponder: students reason why hill roads wind in gentle slopes rather than going straight up, and why a leaning ladder is easier to climb than a vertical pole. They connect both answers to MA = L/h and the trade-off between force and distance.

periods.teacher_notes: The measurement activity works best if each group uses the same cart and plank but different stack heights; consistent apparatus lets students attribute force changes to slope alone. A common experimental difficulty is maintaining constant speed while pulling — remind students to pull steadily and read the spring balance while moving, not while stationary. Watch for students who report that a steeper incline requires less force, which contradicts the MA = L/h formula; this usually means they measured height rather than length of the plank.
homework: A ramp is 2.5 m long and raises a load to a height of 0.5 m. Calculate the mechanical advantage and state the force needed to push a 200 N load up the ramp at constant speed (ignore friction). Then explain what would happen to the required force if the ramp length were increased to 5 m while the height stayed the same.

periods.activity_title: The Lever Principle — Small Effort Over Long Arm Lifts Heavy Load
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of lever with fulcrum, load arm, and effort arm labelled

time_bands.activity: Students set up Activity 7.4: balance the ruler on the pencil. Place the stapler close to the fulcrum (load side). Students add erasers one at a time to the far end and record how many erasers at what distance are needed to lift the stapler. They note that fewer erasers are needed when placed farther from the fulcrum.

Teacher derives the lever principle from the work-energy theorem on the board: effort × d₁ = load × d₂, so MA = effort arm ÷ load arm. Students apply this to the seesaw example from the textbook (15 kg child at 2 m, 30 kg child at 1 m) to verify that the system balances.

Students classify levers from the textbook: scissors (Class I), lemon squeezer (Class II), tweezers (Class III). For each, they draw a diagram placing F (fulcrum), L (load), E (effort) in the correct order and compute a sample MA. Teacher checks that students understand why Class III levers have MA < 1 and still have a use (multiplying distance/speed, not force).

Pause and Ponder: students reason why a spoon used to open a can lid is a lever, why hard objects should be pushed close to a scissors' fulcrum, and why perpetual motion machines cannot work. They connect the last question to the energy-conservation principle established earlier in the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived MA = L/h for the inclined plane from the work-energy theorem, the lever follows the same logic — work in = work out, so F₁d₁ = F₂d₂. A common error in classification is placing Class I and Class II levers in the wrong category; a reliable check is asking: 'Where is the fulcrum relative to load and effort?' before assigning the class. Class III levers often surprise students (MA < 1 seems useless until they realise the output moves farther and faster than the input).

periods.activity_title: Beam Balance Experiment — Measuring the Lever Principle Quantitatively
materials: Ruler (30 cm) with holes or marks at regular intervals
String to suspend ruler at centre
Two small paper cups with strings
Coins of the same denomination (as consistent mass units)

time_bands.activity: Students construct the beam balance from Activity 7.5: suspend the ruler at its midpoint, hang paper cups at equal distances and verify balance. Students then add one coin to the left cup and adjust the right cup's distance to rebalance, recording the distance and coin count for each configuration.

Students systematically vary the number of coins on each side and record: coins on left (n₁), distance from fulcrum on left (d₁), coins on right (n₂), distance on right (d₂). They compute n₁ × d₁ and n₂ × d₂ for each trial and note whether the products are equal.

Students write the lever principle in symbolic form from their data: effort × effort arm = load × load arm. Teacher formalises this and shows it is the same as F₁d₁ = F₂d₂. Students use their data to calculate the MA of one configuration and verify using the formula MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

Consolidation: students answer — machines do not create energy. Using their beam-balance data, they calculate the work done on both sides for one trial (force × distance) and verify that the values are equal (or near-equal with friction), confirming the work-conservation principle in a lever.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the quantitative companion to the qualitative ruler-and-eraser activity — students move from observation to measurement and derivation. Ensure students use the same coins throughout a trial so mass is consistent; mixed coins break the proportionality. A probing question: ask what would happen to the balance if one cup hung at the exact centre (zero arm) — this tests whether students understand that zero distance gives zero torque regardless of load.

periods.activity_title: Applying Conservation of Energy to Kinetic and Potential Energy Problems
periods.visual_aids: Board energy bar diagrams showing KE and PE at different heights

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws an energy bar diagram on the board for a ball falling from height h: at the top, the bar is all PE and the KE bar is zero; at the bottom, reversed. Students sketch the bar diagram for an intermediate height, splitting PE and KE proportionally. This visual representation of E = KE + PE = constant is the entry point.

Students tackle a set of three calculation problems applying conservation of mechanical energy (no friction): (a) find speed at three-quarters of the way down a ramp; (b) find the maximum height a ball thrown upward with speed v will reach; (c) a ball on a roller-coaster loses 10% of its mechanical energy to friction per peak — find the height of the second and third peaks given a starting height of 20 m.

Students compare their answers and resolve disagreements. For the friction problem, students explain in writing why each successive peak is lower, connecting energy dissipation to heat generated by friction — linking the chapter's physics to the observation that real pendulums and roller coasters always fall short.

Teacher draws a connection to the gharat (water mill) described in the chapter's Bridging Science and Society box: water descends from height (PE → KE), drives a wheel (KE → mechanical work), grinding grain. Students identify the energy transformations and connect to the law of conservation of energy.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit revisits conservation of mechanical energy with harder problems that require multi-step reasoning — use it to consolidate before the assessment. The energy bar diagram is a powerful representation for students who struggle with the algebra alone; it makes the constant total visible. Watch for students who add KE and PE at the start and at the end without setting them equal to the same fixed total — the key skill is writing E_total = KE + PE = constant and then solving.

periods.activity_title: Work, Power, and Energy — Multi-Step Problem Solving Across Sections
periods.section_anchor: 7.1 Work Done by a Constant Force / 7.5 Power

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a bridging scenario: a construction crane lifts a 500 kg beam from ground level to the top of a 40 m building, then holds it steady for 30 s, then lowers it halfway. Students identify which phases involve positive work, zero work, and negative work before calculating anything.

Students solve three connected questions about the crane scenario: (a) calculate work done during the lift; (b) calculate work done during the stationary hold; (c) if the lift takes 20 s, calculate the crane's power output; (d) calculate work done during the lowering phase and determine the sign. Students work individually then compare with a partner.

Teacher introduces a second scenario: a car of mass 800 kg travels at constant velocity (no acceleration) — a student claims the engine is doing no work since KE is constant. Students argue whether this claim is correct by identifying the forces (engine force vs. friction/air resistance) and determining the work done by each.

Class discussion consolidates the distinction: when net work is zero (KE constant), individual forces can still do positive and negative work. Teacher uses W = ΔE and the individual-force perspective together to reconcile the apparent contradiction.

periods.teacher_notes: Having studied work, power, and energy conservation in separate units, this problem-solving session requires students to decide which concept applies at each phase of a scenario — that decision-making is the key skill being developed. The constant-velocity car scenario surfaces a genuine misconception: students often reason that constant KE means no work is done at all; the multi-force perspective (engine does positive work, friction does equal negative work) is the correction. Encourage students to list all forces acting before deciding which ones do work.

periods.activity_title: Mechanical Advantage Across All Three Simple Machines — Comparison and Application
periods.visual_aids: Board comparison table of three simple machines

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a three-column comparison table (pulley, inclined plane, lever) on the board with rows: MA formula, how MA > 1 is achieved, trade-off (what increases as force decreases), real-life example. Students fill in the table using their notes and textbook, working in pairs.

Students solve a set of application problems, one per machine: (a) a movable pulley system is used to lift a 600 N load — what effort force is needed, and how far must the effort rope be pulled to raise the load 3 m? (b) a ramp 4 m long raises a load 0.8 m — find MA and the effort to push a 500 N crate; (c) a Class I lever has an effort arm of 1.5 m and a load arm of 0.3 m — find MA and the load it can lift with 40 N effort.

Students compare the three machines across one criterion: which provides the greatest MA? They reason that MA depends on design ratios (L/h, effort arm/load arm, number of supporting rope segments), not on the type of machine, and that any machine can theoretically achieve very high MA by adjusting its geometry — at the cost of a larger effort displacement.

Pause and Ponder consolidation: students answer in writing why no simple machine reduces the total work done, even though each reduces the required effort force. They connect this to the work-energy theorem: total work in = total work out (ideal machines), which is why work, not force, is conserved.

periods.teacher_notes: Having studied each machine separately, this unit requires students to abstract the shared principle — MA > 1 always means effort moves farther than load — across three different physical implementations. Students sometimes believe that a more complex machine (like a compound pulley) violates work conservation; reinforce that every extra rope segment that halves the force doubles the distance the effort rope travels. The comparison table is a useful scaffold for students who struggle to see the pattern without a side-by-side structure.

periods.activity_title: Energy Transformations in Traditional and Modern Technology — Connecting the Chapter
periods.section_anchor: 7.3 Forms of Energy / 7.4.3 Conservation of mechanical energy / 7.6 Simple Machines
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image or teacher-drawn diagram of a gharat (water mill) and a hydroelectric dam

time_bands.activity: Students read the Bridging Science and Society box on the gharat (panchakki) independently. They identify: (a) the energy form at the start (water at height = gravitational PE), (b) the conversion as water falls (PE → KE), (c) the conversion in the wheel (KE → mechanical work), and (d) the modern analogue in hydroelectric dams (KE → electrical energy).

Students draw an annotated energy-flow diagram for both systems (gharat and dam), labelling each conversion step with the form of energy and the machine or component responsible. They include labels for: height of water source, falling water, rotating wheel, millstone or turbine, electrical generator (dam only).

Teacher leads a discussion connecting the gharat to the chapter: the falling water is a lever/inclined-plane analogue (gravity force acts over height); energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted. Students identify which simple machine concept (effort, load, MA) is most applicable to the wheel-and-millstone system and justify their choice.

Students write a paragraph (five to eight sentences) explaining to a younger student why a dam is a practical application of the conservation of mechanical energy, using at least three technical terms from the chapter (gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, work, power, mechanical energy).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to synthesise by applying energy concepts to a real engineering context — traditional and modern. The gharat connects conservation of energy to technology students may not have encountered formally, reinforcing that physics underlies both. Watch for students who describe the energy chain as linear and terminal (energy 'used up'); push them to account for every form the energy takes and identify where losses go (heat, sound), connecting to the earlier observation that real machines always lose some mechanical energy.

questions.question_text: A force of 20 N acts on an object and the object moves 3 m in the direction of the force. On a force-displacement graph for this situation, the area under the graph represents which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: The force multiplied by time

options.label: B
options.text: The power delivered to the object

options.label: C
options.text: The velocity of the object

options.label: D
options.text: The work done on the object, equal to 60 J

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the graphical area with kinematic quantities; does not connect area-under-force-displacement-graph to work.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses work with power; does not distinguish between the quantity computed from F × s and the rate quantity P = W/t.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Applies the impulse formula (F × t) instead of the work formula (F × s); conflates displacement with time on the horizontal axis.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract graph representation can re-read the W = F × s definition and verify numerically: 20 N × 3 m = 60 J. Verbal explainers can state 'force times displacement gives work' to reach the same answer.

questions.question_text: A person carries a heavy bag across a flat room, holding it at a constant height with an upward force equal to the bag's weight, while walking horizontally from one wall to the other. Which statement correctly describes the scientific work done by the person on the bag during this journey?

options.label: A
options.text: Work done is negative because the person's muscles are losing energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Work done is positive because the person exerts a force and the bag moves.

options.label: C
options.text: Work done is zero because the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

options.label: D
options.text: Work done is zero because the person exerts no force on the bag.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies the colloquial meaning of work — any effort with movement — rather than the scientific criterion that force must be in the direction of displacement.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates physiological energy expenditure with scientific work done on the external object; muscle energy loss is real but is not work done on the bag.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies the zero-force condition incorrectly; the person does exert an upward force on the bag, but the bag's displacement is horizontal, making force perpendicular to displacement.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who confuse the three zero-work conditions can draw vectors: one arrow pointing upward (force) and one pointing sideways (displacement), making the perpendicularity visible. Students stronger in algebra can verify using W = F × s × cos θ with θ = 90°.

questions.question_text: A goalkeeper exerts a force of 200 N on a football over a displacement of 0.15 m to stop it. The football was initially moving toward the goalkeeper. (a) State whether the work done by the goalkeeper on the football is positive or negative, and justify your answer using the direction of force relative to displacement. (b) By Newton's third law, the football also exerts a force on the goalkeeper's hands. State whether this work is positive or negative and explain why it has the opposite sign.
expected_elements: Part (a): Identifies that the goalkeeper's force is directed backward (opposite to the football's motion/displacement), so work done = −200 × 0.15 = −30 J; states the sign is negative because force and displacement are in opposite directions.

Part (b): Identifies the reaction force (football on goalkeeper's hands) acts in the direction of the goalkeeper's displacement (hands move backward with the ball), so this work is positive; explains the sign reversal using Newton's third law — action and reaction forces are equal and opposite, so when one does negative work the other does positive work.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the algebraic sign confusing can draw a diagram with labelled arrows: one for the ball's displacement, one for the goalkeeper's force, and one for the reaction force — the arrow directions make the sign visible without algebra. Students comfortable with vectors can use W = F·s·cosθ with θ = 180° for the negative case.

questions.question_text: In a carrom game, a striker hits a white coin, which then hits a black coin. Using the work-energy theorem (W = ΔE) and Newton's third law, trace the energy transfers through this sequence. For each collision, state: (a) which object does positive work and which does negative work, and (b) what happens to the energy of each object involved.
expected_elements: Collision 1 (striker and white coin): The striker exerts a forward force on the white coin — positive work is done on the white coin, its energy increases. The white coin exerts an equal and opposite force on the striker — negative work is done on the striker, its energy decreases.

Collision 2 (white coin and black coin): The white coin exerts a forward force on the black coin — positive work on the black coin, black coin's energy increases. The black coin exerts a backward force on the white coin — negative work on the white coin, white coin's energy decreases.
Correctly applies W = ΔE: positive work → energy gained; negative work → energy lost.
Cites Newton's third law as the basis for the sign reversal at each collision.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the chain difficult to track verbally can draw a sequence of three boxes (striker → white coin → black coin) with arrows labelled + or − to represent work done, and then translate each arrow into an energy statement. Students who are strong in writing can produce a narrative without the diagram.

questions.question_text: A person eats food and then pedals a bicycle up a hill. Which sequence correctly describes the energy conversions that occur from eating to reaching the top of the hill?

options.label: A
options.text: Chemical energy → mechanical energy → kinetic energy + potential energy (with some thermal energy lost to friction)

options.label: B
options.text: Chemical energy → thermal energy → mechanical energy → sound energy

options.label: C
options.text: Electrical energy → chemical energy → mechanical energy → kinetic energy

options.label: D
options.text: Mechanical energy → chemical energy → kinetic energy → potential energy

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the starting form — places mechanical energy before chemical energy, suggesting the student has not identified food as the chemical energy source.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Inserts electrical energy as a starting form, which is not present in biological processes; reflects confusion with an electrical-device energy chain.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Skips mechanical energy and terminates in sound energy, showing that the student cannot complete the chain beyond a single thermal step and has not connected pedalling to either kinetic or potential energy.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with multi-step chains can build the answer step by step: 'What form does food store?' → chemical. 'What do muscles do with it?' → mechanical. 'What does moving on a slope give?' → kinetic and potential. Verbal reasoners can narrate each step before matching it to a form.

questions.question_text: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is bowled from rest and reaches a speed of 43 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate its kinetic energy at this speed using K = ½mv². (b) If the speed is doubled to 86 m s⁻¹, by what factor does the kinetic energy change? Show your reasoning by expressing the ratio K₂/K₁ in terms of the speeds.
expected_elements: Part (a): Correctly substitutes m = 0.16 kg and v = 43 m s⁻¹ into K = ½mv²; calculates K = 0.5 × 0.16 × 43² = 0.5 × 0.16 × 1849 ≈ 147.9 J (accept 147–148 J).
Part (b): Writes K₂/K₁ = (½mv₂²)/(½mv₁²) = v₂²/v₁² = (86)²/(43)² = 4; states that doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy; demonstrates algebraic cancellation of ½ and m.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the proportionality reasoning difficult can compute K for both speeds numerically and then divide; this gives the factor without algebraic cancellation. Students confident in algebra should show the symbolic cancellation in part (b) to demonstrate understanding of why the factor is always v²-dependent.

questions.question_text: A heavy ball is dropped into loose sand from a height of 1 m, creating a depression of depth d. The same ball is then dropped from a height of 2 m. Which of the following best predicts and explains the outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: The depression is deeper than d, because the ball stored more gravitational potential energy at the greater height and transferred more energy to the sand.

options.label: B
options.text: The depression is exactly 2d, because potential energy is directly proportional to height and the work done on the sand doubles exactly.

options.label: C
options.text: The depression is shallower than d, because the ball falls faster from greater height and spends less time in contact with the sand.

options.label: D
options.text: The depression is the same depth d, because the ball's weight does not change.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Focuses on the ball's weight (constant) and ignores the role of height in determining stored energy; does not apply U = mgh.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Correctly predicts a deeper depression and correctly states U ∝ h, but over-claims that the depression depth doubles exactly — the depression depth depends on the sand's resistance, which may not be linear. This distractor rewards correct reasoning about direction while testing whether students over-extend the proportionality.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the relationship — greater height means greater impact energy, not less; this error likely stems from thinking about contact time rather than energy.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can apply U = mgh numerically for both heights and compare: U₂ = mg × 2 = 2U₁, confirming more energy is stored and transferred. Students who reason qualitatively can argue: the ball fell farther, so gravity did more work on it, giving it more energy to transfer.

questions.question_text: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved ramp of height 4 m. (a) Calculate the speed of the ball at the bottom of the ramp, showing each step in your application of conservation of mechanical energy. (b) In a real experiment, the ball's measured speed at the bottom is 8.5 m s⁻¹ instead of the value you calculated. Identify the cause of this discrepancy and explain, using the concept of mechanical energy, what happened to the 'missing' energy. (c) A student claims that the ball's speed at the bottom would be greater if the ramp were steeper but the same height. Evaluate this claim using conservation of mechanical energy.
look_for: Part (a): Sets up E_top = E_bottom, i.e. mgh = ½mv²; correctly cancels m; solves v = √(2 × 10 × 4) = √80 ≈ 8.94 m s⁻¹ (using g = 10 m s⁻²). Shows algebraic steps explicitly.

Part (b): Identifies friction (between ball and ramp surface) and/or air resistance as the cause. Explains that mechanical energy was partially converted to thermal energy (heat); the 'missing' energy was dissipated, not destroyed — total energy is still conserved, but not all in mechanical form.

Part (c): Correctly evaluates the claim as false; since conservation of mechanical energy gives v = √(2gh) and this depends only on h (not on the ramp shape or steepness), the speed at the bottom is the same for any smooth ramp of the same height. A strong response cites v = √(2gh) explicitly and notes that shape affects only the path, not the energy available.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with part (c) can first compute v for two different ramp angles of the same height numerically and notice they get the same answer, then explain why in words. Students who are algebraically confident should arrive at the independence directly from v = √(2gh) without needing numerical examples.

questions.question_text: A student of mass 50 kg climbs a staircase of vertical height 6 m in 15 seconds. (a) Calculate the work done by the student against gravity and then calculate the student's average power output during the climb (use g = 10 m s⁻²). (b) A second student of the same mass climbs the same staircase more slowly, taking 30 seconds. Compare the total work done and the average power for the two students, explaining why the two quantities differ in their comparison.
expected_elements: Part (b): Total work is the same for both students (3000 J each) because both lift the same mass to the same height. Power is different: second student's power = 3000/30 = 100 W, which is half the first student's power. Explanation: total work depends only on force and displacement; power depends on how quickly the work is done, so the same work done in twice the time gives half the power.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who conflate work and power can annotate their calculation with units at each step: joules for work, seconds for time, watts for power — the units keep the two quantities distinct. Students who find the comparison conceptually unclear can use the analogy from the section: two workers carry the same load up the same stairs, one faster — neither does more work, but one requires greater power.

questions.question_text: A simple machine has a mechanical advantage of 5. A student claims that using this machine means less total work needs to be done to lift a heavy object. Which response correctly evaluates this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct — a higher mechanical advantage always reduces total work.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct — the machine converts some of the load's weight into a form that requires no work.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is incorrect — machines always increase total work because friction wastes some energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is incorrect — the machine reduces the effort force required, but the effort must be applied over a distance five times greater than the load moves, keeping total work the same.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Holds the common misconception that machines reduce total work; does not apply the work-conservation principle (effort × effort-distance = load × load-distance).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a mechanism ('converts weight into a form that requires no work') that has no basis in the chapter; indicates the student has not understood that energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly identifies that machines do not reduce total work (getting the direction right) but gives friction as the reason — friction increases work input, it does not maintain work conservation in an ideal machine. This distractor catches students who know machines have friction losses but confuse the ideal-case argument with the real-case argument.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can verify with a numerical example: if MA = 5 and load = 100 N, effort = 20 N; if load moves 1 m, effort rope moves 5 m; work on load = 100 J, work by effort = 20 × 5 = 100 J — same total. This concrete check makes the principle tangible.

questions.question_text: A fixed pulley is used to lift a 200 N load, and a movable pulley system (with a single movable pulley) is used to lift the same load. Which of the following correctly describes the effort force and effort distance for each system?

options.label: A
options.text: Both systems require 200 N of effort, but the movable pulley changes the direction of pull.

options.label: B
options.text: Fixed pulley: effort = 100 N, effort-rope pulled 2 m. Movable pulley: effort = 200 N, effort-rope pulled 1 m.

options.label: C
options.text: Fixed pulley: effort = 200 N, effort-rope pulled 1 m for every 1 m the load rises. Movable pulley: effort = 100 N, effort-rope pulled 2 m for every 1 m the load rises.

options.label: D
options.text: Fixed pulley: effort = 200 N, effort-rope pulled 2 m. Movable pulley: effort = 100 N, effort-rope pulled 1 m.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reverses the properties of the two pulley types — assigns MA > 1 to the fixed pulley and MA = 1 to the movable; indicates the student has confused the two configurations.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Correctly identifies that the movable pulley halves the force, but doubles the effort distance for the fixed pulley instead — suggesting partial knowledge without the work-conservation constraint.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Assigns the direction-change advantage to the movable pulley rather than the fixed pulley; confuses which configuration changes direction without changing force magnitude.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the two-rope argument for movable pulleys can draw a diagram showing the load supported by two rope segments; each segment bears half the load, so effort = load/2. Students who find the direction-change concept abstract can think of a flag hoist, which is a familiar fixed-pulley application.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Ramp configuration | Length (L) | Height (h) | MA = L/h
Ramp P | 3.0 m | 0.5 m | ?
Ramp Q | 1.5 m | 0.5 m | ?
Ramp R | 6.0 m | 0.5 m | ?
questions.question_text: Three ramps all raise a load to the same height of 0.5 m but have different lengths. Refer to the table provided. (a) Calculate the mechanical advantage (MA = L/h) for each ramp and complete the table. (b) A warehouse worker needs to push a 300 N crate up a ramp to a shelf 0.5 m high. Using Ramp R, calculate the effort force required (ignore friction). (c) The worker prefers Ramp R over Ramp Q. Using the MA formula and the work-energy theorem, explain why a longer ramp requires less effort force, and state what the worker must accept as the trade-off.
expected_elements: Part (a): MA for Ramp P = 3.0/0.5 = 6; Ramp Q = 1.5/0.5 = 3; Ramp R = 6.0/0.5 = 12.

Part (c): Derives from F′ × L = mg × h that F′ = mgh/L; as L increases (with h fixed), F′ decreases — longer ramp gives smaller effort. Trade-off: the effort must be applied over a greater distance (Ramp R requires pushing over 6 m instead of 1.5 m for Ramp Q), so total work remains mgh = 150 J regardless of ramp choice.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find part (c) difficult can calculate work done by effort for each ramp (effort × L) and verify it equals 150 J in all cases, letting the numerical pattern lead to the verbal explanation. Students comfortable with algebra can derive the relationship F′ = mgh/L directly to make the inverse proportionality explicit.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates the principle of mechanical advantage by constructing simple machines.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Trial | Coins on left (n₁) | Distance from fulcrum — left (d₁, cm) | Coins on right (n₂) | Distance from fulcrum — right (d₂, cm) | n₁ × d₁ | n₂ × d₂
1 | 2 | 10 | 4 | ? | 20 | ?
2 | 3 | 8 | ? | 6 | 24 | ?
3 | 5 | 4 | 2 | ? | 20 | ?
questions.task: The table shows partial data from a beam-balance experiment. In each trial, a ruler was balanced on a pencil at its midpoint, and paper cups holding coins were hung at measured distances from the fulcrum. (a) Complete the missing values in the table using the lever principle F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ (here, n₁d₁ = n₂d₂ since coin mass is constant). (b) Using the completed table, state the lever principle in your own words and explain what the products in the last two columns tell you about energy conservation in a lever. (c) A student proposes using a lever to lift a 60 N rock using only 15 N of effort. Determine the minimum effort arm length needed if the load arm is 0.4 m, and classify the lever if the fulcrum is placed between the effort and the load.
questions.scaffold: For part (a): the product n₁ × d₁ must equal n₂ × d₂ for the lever to balance. Find the unknown n or d by dividing the known product by the known quantity. For part (c): use MA = effort arm / load arm = load / effort, and identify the positions of fulcrum, load, and effort to name the lever class.
format_of_output: Completed table with all missing values filled in and n₁d₁ and n₂d₂ calculated.
A written statement of the lever principle in the student's own words (two to three sentences).
An explanation of what equal products in the last two columns mean in terms of work and energy.
Calculation of the minimum effort arm length for part (c) with working shown.
Identification of the lever class with justification based on the positions of fulcrum, load, and effort.

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's core skill is deriving the lever principle from systematic measurement; a data table with missing values directly tests whether students can apply n₁d₁ = n₂d₂ to fill gaps, state the principle, and connect equal products to energy conservation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate that they can read experimental data, apply the lever principle quantitatively, interpret the conservation implication of equal work-products, design a lever for a given mechanical advantage, and classify the lever by component positions.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to recognise that each row is a balance equation; students who cannot immediately see the missing value should isolate the unknown by dividing the known product by the known quantity. The lever classification hint directs students to the spatial arrangement criterion rather than to memorised class names.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses complete the table correctly, state the principle as 'effort times effort arm equals load times load arm' (or equivalent), explicitly connect equal products to equal work done on both sides (energy conservation), show the MA calculation algebraically in part (c), and correctly identify the lever as Class I. Weak responses complete the table by pattern without articulating the principle, omit the energy conservation link, or misclassify the lever by confusing the position of the fulcrum.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstraction of 'coins as force units' can re-read the section's derivation using actual force values (F₁d₁ = F₂d₂) and note that using identical coins makes coin count proportional to force — this unpacks the experimental shorthand. Students who find part (b)'s energy connection difficult can calculate effort × effort-arm for one trial and compare it to load × load-arm numerically before writing the verbal explanation.
